At the end of June, we lost access to GPT-5.6 Sol while it went through government review. Dan Shipper https://every. said returning to older models felt like going back to the Stone Age. Austin Tedesco https://every.to/emails/click/136f006095268802530f927779a5f4d55a493840c0f1f77c950761a77b64df9e/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiVmliZSBDaGVjazogR1BULTUuNiBTb2wgSXMgT3VyIEZhdm9yaXRlIE1vZGVsIHRvIENvbGxhYm9yYXRlIFdpdGgiLCJwb3N0X2lkIjo0MzM1LCJwb3N0X3R5cGUiOiJwb3N0IiwidXJsIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9AdGVkZXNjYXUiLCJwb3NpdGlvbiI6N30= compared GPT-5.5 to shooting a basketball twice as heavy.

Now Sol is back, alongside OpenAI’s new unified ChatGPT and Codex desktop app. OpenAI calls it the company’s strongest model yet. Our verdict is narrower: Fable still gets the biggest, loosest assignments. Sol is the model most of us want open all day.

We tested it across coding, writing, research, spreadsheets, and agent workflows. The results include a few contradictions worth understanding:

 * Why Sol’s Senior Engineer score tells a complicated story about persistence, skill, and restraint
 * How one of the weakest one-shot writers in our benchmark became my (Katie Parrott https://every.’s) favorite model to write with
 * The spreadsheet test that made Arielle Shipper feel the magic of Sol—and then gave her whiplash
 * When the Every team routes a job to Sol, Fable, or Opus

Sol changes the feel of everyday knowledge work. It finds the files, holds onto the context, and produces another pass while the decision is still fresh in your mind.
